scope: Project-owned synthetic authoring baseline for third author revision, before any clinical/source edit. No player data or external source text.

review.title: HIDA after equivocal gallbladder ultrasound
fairness: Review scope: all 43 main items plus all 30 embedded contextRevisions are included. Judgments use only current after Presentation, Current update, Exhibit, Task and Options, with the key marker hidden for cue assessment; titles and first-pass notes are identifiers/comparison data, not evidence for the current key. Author self-checks, reviewResponse claims, future results and feedback were not used to justify answers. Difficulty is an uncalibrated PGY-2/3 prediction. Indexed first-pass notes below cover every cue, fairness note and suggestion; UPHELD marks an earlier positive observation, and UNRESOLVED/PARTLY RESOLVED identify remaining defects.

Acute inflammatory symptoms despite incomplete sonographic inflammatory findings must be interpreted, then gallbladder-filling assessment distinguished from stimulated emptying and duct imaging. This is meaningful protocol selection; the key is defensible among these three choices.

Normal bilirubin and a nondilated duct favor the intended question but do not rule out every duct disorder. These are purposeful observations, not a lay-language elimination. Two scintigraphy choices create a shortlist but do not select the key without knowledge.

Offline editorial review only: no sources verified, no clinician approval conferred. The same limitation applies to every entry in this report; PASS means passes this wording/difficulty review, and clinical judgments remain needs_clinician_review.
First-pass fairness[1]: UPHELD: the actual ultrasound observations remain unlabelled.
First-pass fairness[2]: RESOLVED for the offered set: acute inflammatory findings and separate filling/ejection protocols now focus the decision; generic CT is removed.

First-pass fairness[3]: PARTLY RESOLVED: duct caliber and bilirubin are supplied. Clinical inspiratory arrest is not a documented sonographic Murphy result; that distinction should be preserved, although it does not defeat this narrower option set.
First-pass suggestions[1]: RESOLVED editorially: acute concern and protocol alternatives now supply the distinction. Named clinician confirmation is not ascertainable from allowed fields.
First-pass suggestions[2]: RESOLVED: MRCP is explicitly named and all choices specify the assessed function/anatomy.
First-pass suggestions[3]: RESOLVED: no summary label or announced need for HIDA.
suggestions: Retain the raw examination and ultrasound data and verify the protocol ranking with Melissa; do not reintroduce an 'inconclusive' label.

review.title: Classify nipple discharge patterns

cues.phrase: Breast assessment and medication review
cues.why: Only the key assesses the organ that produces the presenting symptom; the other plans both divert to medication/endocrine follow-up. A lay reader can select the broad breast-plus-medication plan without integrating the findings.

cues.phrase: red-brown drop
cues.why: Everyday concern about blood points toward breast evaluation. This is clinically necessary information; the weak option set, not the observation, needs repair.

fairness: The spontaneous unilateral component warrants breast evaluation even with a plausible drug-associated bilateral component; the key is defensible as a broad plan.

Two judgments are possible, but neither is difficult here: do not let the elevated prolactin explain away the focal discharge. 'Breast assessment' is too broad to demonstrate a resident-level evaluation decision.
First-pass cues[1]: PARTLY RESOLVED: the word 'pathologic' is gone, but blood-colored discharge still shortcuts the only breast-assessment plan.
First-pass cues[2]: RESOLVED: galactorrhea versus broad categories is replaced by parallel plan categories.
First-pass fairness[1]: UPHELD: the mixed pattern remains clinically meaningful.
First-pass fairness[2]: PARTLY RESOLVED: task no longer explicitly selects the concerning component; consequential plan selection is added, but remains easy.
First-pass fairness[3]: UPHELD: no confident new inaccuracy; endocrine findings need not explain the focal component.
First-pass suggestions[1]: PARTLY RESOLVED: evaluation replaces classification, but the breast-only-in-key shortcut limits discrimination.
First-pass suggestions[2]: RESOLVED by changing the objective to evaluation; the three plans are categories of management, though still too broad.
suggestions: Compare three concrete same-stage breast/endocrine evaluation plans that all address the breast complaint; make the decision depend on which tests or follow-up the mixed findings actually warrant.
Keep the medication and observed discharge patterns; do not remove blood color merely to disguise risk.

review.title: Select diagnostic imaging for pathologic discharge
fairness: The initial stage is now explicit and all options contain two imaging modalities. No reliable nonmedical cue selects the key.

Interpreting the mixed discharge and selecting conventional initial imaging at age 42 is a simple two-step chain, likely too easy for PGY-2/3 residents. The two MRI bundles chiefly test the same premature-MRI error.
The key is defensible; no confident clinical inaccuracy identified in the allowed fields.
First-pass cues[1]: RESOLVED: all choices pair tests and the diagnostic-versus-screening shortcut is removed.
First-pass cues[2]: RESOLVED: the repeated persistence update is replaced by prior-imaging status.
First-pass fairness[1]: UPHELD: age and focal spontaneous component support the initial pathway.
First-pass fairness[2]: PARTLY RESOLVED: packaging is repaired, but the chain remains straightforward.
First-pass fairness[3]: RESOLVED: no breast imaging has yet been performed.
First-pass suggestions[1]: RESOLVED: initial stage explicit without naming a preferred modality.
First-pass suggestions[2]: RESOLVED: parallel two-test pathways.
First-pass suggestions[3]: RESOLVED: spontaneous history kept without duplicate persistence update.
suggestions: Use a verified discordant prior-imaging result and a consequential next decision, or retain this as a separately accepted foundational imaging item.
Give each distractor a distinct credible misconception rather than using MRI twice as the common wrong component.

review.title: Perioperative ART continuity

cues.phrase: the anesthesia service can administer and monitor intravenous sedation
cues.why: The setting sentence supplies the implementation rationale for the IV half of the key. It closely echoes 'titrated intravenous midazolam with respiratory monitoring' and narrows the four combinations without knowing the interaction.

fairness: The regimen is now consequential: continuity and the route-specific interaction must both be handled. This can be a moderate two-step resident item after removing the setting hint.
The full factorial options are parallel; neither ART continuation nor IV route alone identifies the complete key.
Monitored titration is directionally defensible; exact midazolam/boosted-regimen handling requires named clinician verification. No dosing or interruption interval is inferred.
First-pass fairness[1]: UPHELD: option lengths and component balance remain acceptable, but a new setting cue appears in the stem.
First-pass fairness[2]: RESOLVED: oral midazolam makes the named regimen relevant to the decision.
First-pass fairness[3]: RESOLVED for the intended interaction objective: a planned medication and IV procedural setting are supplied; no oral-access problem is asserted.
First-pass suggestions[1]: RESOLVED: medication-specific combined plans now require both decisions, subject to the new availability cue.
First-pass suggestions[2]: RESOLVED by application redesign; no invented interruption interval.
suggestions: Remove the service-availability sentence unless it is a real necessary constraint; state neutral procedural context sufficient for all offered routes.
Have Melissa verify the exact oral-versus-IV plan and monitoring language, including whether dose adjustment needs to be explicit.

review.title: Boosted ART and midazolam

cues.phrase: more than one intravenous midazolam dose
cues.why: The repeated-dose concern plus smaller/standard increments invites a general 'use less and monitor' heuristic; the question now tests one dose-adjustment rule.

cues.phrase: Consider omitting ritonavir; use standard increments with monitored titration
cues.why: Only this longer option alters a second drug. It is a category/commitment outlier beside two increment choices.

fairness: Recognizing ritonavir and choosing cautious titration is a defensible application, but the current choices reduce it to a familiar single interaction rule; the route is already settled.

Standard increments with monitored titration may encompass cautious individualized dosing unless 'standard' is operationally defined. I cannot certify that these two flexible instructions represent mutually exclusive clinically meaningful plans.
No exact drug dose or duration is asserted; omission of ritonavir must not be taught as immediately removing interaction.
First-pass cues[1]: RESOLVED: vague 'revise sedation' is replaced with a specified adjustment.
First-pass cues[2]: RESOLVED: unexplained escalation removed.
First-pass fairness[1]: PARTLY RESOLVED: drug/route interaction remains, but the task now asks a single incremental-dosing rule.
First-pass fairness[2]: PARTLY RESOLVED: direction of adjustment specified, yet smaller versus standard monitored titration overlaps.
First-pass fairness[3]: PARTLY RESOLVED: omission names ritonavir, but timing and residual effects remain unspecified; it is still a conspicuously different plan.
First-pass suggestions[1]: PARTLY RESOLVED: concrete adjustments replace vague plans, but specificity and actionable distinction need repair.
First-pass suggestions[2]: PARTLY RESOLVED: exact regimen retained; oral proposal persists, though the tested procedure is explicitly IV and the availability cue remains.
First-pass suggestions[3]: RESOLVED for dose escalation; clinician verification of all plans is not established by allowed fields.
suggestions: Compare concrete, clinically verified complete sedation plans at equal specificity, with the same drugs and monitoring components in each.
Use an actual response or accumulation problem that requires interpreting observations before a next-dose decision; avoid unsupported dose values.

review.title: Manometric recognition of achalasia
fairness: The body description depicts simultaneous pressurization without propagation; combined with elevated relaxation pressure it still directly identifies the diagnostic pattern. Translating prose into a diagnosis is one classification, not two consequential steps.

No reliable nonmedical key cue. 'Achalasia' is necessarily shorter than the other diagnostic names; the first-pass shortest-label warning is too weak to justify artificial padding. The likely key is defensible, with the additional classification boundary noted above.
First-pass cues[1]: ACCEPTED, not an actionable defect: the natural short diagnosis remains, with no robust answer-from-length shortcut.
First-pass fairness[1]: UPHELD in broad direction, with the current variant-specific observations and caveats assessed above.
First-pass fairness[2]: UNRESOLVED: richer observations still culminate in one diagnostic classification; likely too easy.
First-pass fairness[3]: UPHELD: structural workup is legitimate context; no new absolute exclusion should be inferred.
First-pass suggestions[1]: UNRESOLVED: still a diagnosis-only resident item rather than a consequential next decision.
First-pass suggestions[2]: PARTLY RESOLVED: pressurization is described, but no real competing interpretation is added.
First-pass suggestions[3]: RESOLVED: siblings now differ in pressurization, position dependence, premature contractions, and low contractile readouts; this alone does not establish difficulty.
suggestions: Add a supported discordant study or subsequent decision instead of expanding prose around the classic defining pair.
Retain the relevant endoscopic workup; do not equate no intraluminal mass with exclusion of every secondary cause.

fairness: After nonobstructing endoscopy, mixed solid/liquid dysphagia suggests a motor process and manometry is the defensible next physiologic study. The chain is genuine but routine and likely too easy for residents.

First-pass fairness[1]: UPHELD: simple symptom-to-physiology-to-test chain.

First-pass fairness[4]: UPHELD: no claim that normal endoscopy excludes every secondary cause.

First-pass suggestions[2]: RESOLVED: raw symptoms/endoscopy retained without a motility label.

review.title: Dynamic ultrasound after an equivocal inguinal-hernia examination
fairness: The intermittent visible/palpable contour change despite a negative office examination supports dynamic evaluation even with a musculoskeletal pain finding. Ultrasound is a defensible initial option; it remains a routine two-step decision for PGY-2/3 residents.

No prior imaging is now explicit and protocol labels are comparable. MRI can address the musculoskeletal component, but its offered hip/adductor protocol does not necessarily adjudicate the reported intermittent protrusion. Clinician review should confirm the intended initial ranking.
The dynamic history is necessary evidence, not a reliable lay lexical match. The added competing pain maneuver does little once a distinct swelling is reported.
First-pass fairness[1]: UPHELD: a genuine but simple occult/reducible-protrusion inference.
First-pass fairness[2]: RESOLVED as to stage: first imaging explicitly stated. Comparative ranking still needs clinician confirmation.
First-pass fairness[3]: PARTLY RESOLVED: standing/Valsalva specified, but resident difficulty remains easy.
First-pass suggestions[1]: RESOLVED: no previous imaging and protocol-level labels supplied.
First-pass suggestions[2]: UNRESOLVED: no prior discordant study; adding a musculoskeletal maneuver has not made the decision difficult.
First-pass suggestions[3]: PARTLY RESOLVED: musculoskeletal findings differ, but all four still report intermittent swelling with the same negative office examination and same first test.
suggestions: Make the competing interpretation consequential with a verified discordant initial study and a specific unresolved clinical problem, or classify the current sequence as foundational.
Ensure all offered protocols could realistically investigate the unresolved problem; do not specify the MRI narrowly simply to make it lose.

review.title: Elective planning for symptomatic inguinal hernia
fairness: The update gives a plainly reducible bowel-containing inguinal protrusion with activity-limiting pain. Interpreting it and discussing repair is a real but elementary two-step chain.
Elective consultation appropriately preserves risk assessment/shared decision-making. The musculoskeletal symptoms may coexist, so consultation should not promise that repair cures all pain.
Watchful waiting and a support garment are both nonoperative symptom strategies; absent competing operative risk, they provide weak discrimination. No reliable key-only wording cue.
First-pass cues[1]: RESOLVED: task no longer declares a confirmed symptomatic hernia or repeats the keyed treatment noun.
First-pass cues[2]: RESOLVED: presumed groin strain is removed.
First-pass cues[3]: RESOLVED: emergency exploration filler removed.
First-pass fairness[1]: UPHELD: elective risk/repair consultation is defensible.
First-pass fairness[2]: UPHELD: activity limitation remains necessary context.
First-pass fairness[3]: PARTLY RESOLVED: ultrasound now supplies observations instead of a diagnostic label; the inference remains obvious and observation is less favored without competing risk.
First-pass suggestions[1]: RESOLVED: all choices address management of the same problem.
First-pass suggestions[2]: UNRESOLVED: the allowed fields do not explicitly present a foundational purpose.

suggestions: Keep reducibility and functional impact; add a verified competing risk/timing issue if a resident-level decision is required.
Give nonoperative alternatives distinct indications rather than two versions of deferring repair; otherwise accept this only as a foundational referral item.

The measured event is never named and lower event risk is never defined as benefit. The protocol 'study decision' also does not specify whether its target is evaluated by point estimate or confidence interval. In B27, those interpretations directly produce different target-benefit conclusions.

revisions.previousStem: Which diagnosis best explains Ella Morgan's focal upper-midline abdominal-wall defect?
revisions.presentationTemplate: Ella Morgan, a {ageYears}-year-old girl, visits the clinic with her mother, Rachel Morgan, who remains in the same room throughout the visit. Her mother points out a small focal lump in Ella's upper abdominal midline. Examination identifies a small abdominal-wall gap with protruding fat at that site, above the navel. Her previous abdominal operation used a right-lower-quadrant incision. Ella is comfortable.
revisions.intendedInference: Localize the defect and relate it to the operative history among competing abdominal-wall hernias.
revisions.reviewerNotes: Still an anatomical-recognition task, with stronger same-category competitors. Confirm pediatric plausibility. Morgagni is diaphragmatic and is excluded from this abdominal-wall option set; no new diagnosis or concept meaning is intended.

question.stem: Which diagnosis best explains Ella Morgan's abdominal-wall lump?

answerChoices.label: Epigastric hernia
answerChoices.rationale: Uses the focal upper-midline fat-containing wall defect; the previous incision is at a different site.

answerChoices.label: Spigelian hernia
answerChoices.rationale: Confuses a lateral abdominal-wall defect near the semilunar line with the observed midline defect.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Confuses a lateral abdominal-wall defect near the semilunar line with the observed midline defect.

answerChoices.label: Incisional hernia
answerChoices.rationale: Overweights the operative history without matching the current defect to the prior incision.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Overweights the operative history without matching the current defect to the prior incision.

answerChoices.label: Lumbar hernia
answerChoices.rationale: Confuses a posterior or flank wall defect with the anterior upper-midline finding.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Confuses a posterior or flank wall defect with the anterior upper-midline finding.

question.explanation: The focal upper-midline fat-containing defect supports epigastric hernia. Spigelian and lumbar defects occupy different abdominal-wall regions; an incisional hernia is related to an operative incision, which is elsewhere in this record. All offered diagnoses are abdominal-wall hernias.

question.stem: Which diagnostic sampling plan should be used for {patientName}'s skin lesion?

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: Atypical B cells expand the gastric lamina propria and infiltrate glands. CD20 and CD79a stain the infiltrate; CD5, CD10 and cyclin D1 do not. The infiltrate contains lymphocytes with irregular nuclei and pale cytoplasm around and within gastric glands.
decisionNodes.stem: Which diagnosis best fits {patientName}'s integrated biopsy findings?

answerChoices.label: Gastric extranodal marginal-zone lymphoma
answerChoices.rationale: Integrates the gland-infiltrating marginal-zone-type architecture and typical B-cell marker profile.

answerChoices.label: Gastric follicular lymphoma
answerChoices.rationale: Requires a different integrated architectural/germinal-center pattern rather than B-cell lineage alone.

answerChoices.label: Gastric mantle-cell lymphoma
answerChoices.rationale: Is a small-B-cell competitor but is not favored by the integrated marker/architectural findings.

decisionNodes.explanation: The architecture and phenotype together support MALT-type extranodal marginal-zone lymphoma. Follicular and mantle-cell lymphoma are closer small-B-cell alternatives than a large-cell label dismissed by a size adjective. Marker exceptions still require integrated pathology review.

cases.learningSummary:
Small B cells infiltrating gastric glands to form lymphoepithelial lesions, with CD20 and CD79a expression and absent CD5, CD10, and cyclin D1, support gastric MALT lymphoma. The morphology and immunophenotype must be interpreted together.

H. pylori eradication is initial lymphoma-directed treatment for this classic localized low-grade presentation. Eradication must be confirmed and lymphoma response reassessed; this is not permission to omit follow-up.

decisionNodes.stem: Which next diagnostic action should classify {patientName}'s infiltrate?

decisionNodes.stem: Which operative plan should be discussed for {patientName}?

answerChoices.label: Gastrectomy with D2 lymphadenectomy and spleen preservation
answerChoices.rationale: Integrates the wall-depth finding with nodal extent while avoiding routine removal of an uninvolved spleen.

answerChoices.label: Gastrectomy with D1 lymphadenectomy and spleen preservation
answerChoices.rationale: Preserves the organ but underestimates the nodal extent appropriate to the represented invasive stage.

answerChoices.label: Gastrectomy with D2 lymphadenectomy and splenic resection
answerChoices.rationale: Provides the nodal extent but adds prophylactic organ removal without a supplied therapeutic indication.

answerChoices.label: Gastrectomy with D1 lymphadenectomy and splenic resection
answerChoices.rationale: Combines an inadequate nodal extent for the represented stage with unindicated splenic removal.

decisionNodes.explanation: The wall-depth observation supports an invasive stage requiring appropriate D2 nodal planning in an experienced service. decisionNodes.stem: Which intervention should complete {patientName}'s endoscopic treatment?

answerChoices.label: Contact bipolar coagulation of the visible vessel
answerChoices.rationale: Adds an appropriate second local modality after injection, when the initial clip attempt has not treated the target.

answerChoices.label: Additional epinephrine injection around the visible vessel
answerChoices.rationale: Repeats the same temporary injection strategy without supplying the necessary additional local modality.

answerChoices.label: Topical hemostatic powder over the visible vessel
answerChoices.rationale: Substitutes a rescue/temporizing agent for the offered suitable contact treatment after control of active oozing.

Topical agents have rescue/temporizing roles and are not treated as interchangeable definitive therapy here.

cases.learningSummary:
Active spurting, active oozing, and a nonbleeding visible vessel are high-risk peptic-ulcer stigmata that warrant endoscopic hemostasis. A clean base or flat pigmented spot does not require endoscopic treatment solely for that finding.

For a nonbleeding visible vessel, accepted thermal or mechanical therapy may be used alone or with epinephrine. Epinephrine alone is not definitive hemostasis, while two definitive modalities are not automatically required.

decisionNodes.stem: Which local characterization study should precede tissue sampling of {patientName}'s mass?

answerChoices.label: Extremity MRI before and after intravenous contrast
answerChoices.rationale: Defines the deep lesion and adjacent compartments before biopsy; ultrasound has not shown its deep extent.

answerChoices.label: Extremity CT before and after intravenous contrast
answerChoices.rationale: Is a plausible cross-sectional alternative but does not replace the preferred soft-tissue local characterization in this setting.

answerChoices.label: Extremity ultrasound with color-flow and spectral Doppler
answerChoices.rationale: Can add vascular information but does not resolve the unvisualized deep extent of this demonstrated subfascial lesion.

answerChoices.label: Region A within the mass
answerChoices.rationale: Targets tissue likely to provide viable diagnostic tumor rather than fluid/necrosis or adjacent reactive change.

decisionNodes.stem: Which motility diagnosis best accounts for {patientName}'s combined study findings?

answerChoices.label: Achalasia
answerChoices.rationale: Integrates the body-pressure/contraction distinction with the appropriate junction-relaxation criterion; an apparent pressure event is not automatically normal peristalsis.

answerChoices.label: Esophagogastric junction outflow obstruction
answerChoices.rationale: Represents a competing motility classification; check whether its relaxation and true-peristalsis requirements fit all of the reported observations.

answerChoices.label: Distal esophageal spasm
answerChoices.rationale: Represents a competing motility classification; check whether its relaxation and true-peristalsis requirements fit all of the reported observations.

decisionNodes.explanation: Simultaneous pressurization does not establish a propagated contraction. Integrating absent true peristalsis with impaired junction relaxation supports achalasia rather than preserved-peristalsis outflow obstruction or spasm.

decisionNodes.stem: Which diagnostic sampling plan should be used for {patientName}'s skin lesion?

answerChoices.label: Elliptical sampling of the lesion through the dermis into subcutaneous fat
answerChoices.rationale: Captures the heterogeneous lesion and a depth adequate for microstaging without committing to definitive wide margins before diagnosis.

answerChoices.label: Punch sampling of the darkest focus through the dermis into subcutaneous fat
answerChoices.rationale: Can provide depth but risks selecting an unrepresentative component of a small heterogeneous lesion that can be sampled in its entirety.

answerChoices.label: Tangential sampling of the lesion across its surface and papillary dermis
answerChoices.rationale: Captures surface extent but risks inadequate depth; this specific shallow plan is not a claim that every saucerization technique is inappropriate.

decisionNodes.explanation: Diagnostic sampling must permit assessment of the heterogeneous lesion and its depth. A narrow diagnostic excision is distinct from the later definitive excision plan; a shallow surface specimen or a selected focus may compromise microstaging.

decisionNodes.stem: Which regional-node plan should accompany {patientName}'s further excision planning?

answerChoices.label: Sentinel lymph node mapping and biopsy
answerChoices.rationale: Interprets the primary depth and clinically uninvolved basin, rather than treating reassuring node imaging as exclusion of microscopic involvement.

answerChoices.label: Ultrasound-guided biopsy of an imaged regional node
answerChoices.rationale: Confuses size-selected sampling of a nonsuspicious visible node with mapping the sentinel drainage of the primary lesion.

answerChoices.label: Ultrasound surveillance of the regional nodes
answerChoices.rationale: Overweights benign-appearing imaged nodes and omits the indicated pathologic sentinel staging discussion.

decisionNodes.explanation: The histology establishes an invasive melanoma with the supplied depth. In this clinically node-negative setting, sentinel-node staging should be discussed with definitive excision planning; sampling an arbitrary benign-appearing node or relying on surveillance does not supply equivalent sentinel staging.

cases.learningSummary: A small accessible lesion concerning for melanoma is usually removed completely with narrow clinical margins and enough depth for histologic microstaging. Selected large or difficult lesions can require a different biopsy approach. Intermediate-thickness invasive melanoma with no clinically palpable nodes supports discussion of sentinel lymph-node biopsy for pathological regional staging. This is distinct from automatic complete nodal dissection and does not guarantee a survival benefit.

decisionNodes.explanation: The pathology, not the scar's appearance, establishes the need for invasive-cancer staging. CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis is a standard initial pathway. decisionNodes.stem: Which examination protocol should evaluate {patientName}'s persistent upper-abdominal symptoms?

answerChoices.label: CT abdomen with intravenous contrast
answerChoices.rationale: Evaluates the pancreatic region, tissue enhancement and anatomic relationships when a post-pancreatitis complication is suspected.

answerChoices.label: CT abdomen with oral luminal contrast
answerChoices.rationale: Outlines the bowel but does not provide the same enhancement/vascular assessment of a pancreatic-region complication.

answerChoices.label: CT abdomen without contrast material
answerChoices.rationale: Can depict some findings, but does not provide equivalent tissue-enhancement information for characterizing the suspected complication.

decisionNodes.explanation: Persistent symptoms after pancreatitis require evaluation of possible structural complications. Contrast-enhanced CT characterizes the pancreatic region and its relationships; oral contrast or a noncontrast survey does not replace intravenous enhancement. MRI can also be appropriate in selected circumstances and is not offered as a falsely invalid alternative.

decisionNodes.stem: Which management plan should be recommended for {patientName}'s returned imaging findings and ongoing symptoms?

answerChoices.label: Referral for endoscopic transmural drainage assessment
answerChoices.rationale: Retains the passed anatomy/symptom inference while requiring specialist assessment of vascular/access safety before any puncture.

answerChoices.label: Referral for percutaneous catheter drainage assessment
answerChoices.rationale: Is a possible route in selected circumstances, but is not favored over endoscopic assessment for the supplied gastric apposition and burden.

answerChoices.label: Referral for operative internal drainage assessment
answerChoices.rationale: May be appropriate in selected anatomy or after other approaches fail; no such preference is established here.

answerChoices.label: Observation with nutritional support and repeat imaging
answerChoices.rationale: Is appropriate for some collections, but does not address the represented ongoing gastric compression/food-intake burden as well as specialist drainage planning.

decisionNodes.explanation: The post-interstitial-pancreatitis history and walled fluid-only collection support pseudocyst classification. Persistent symptoms and gastric apposition support referral for EUS-guided drainage when feasible; no size-only or exact elapsed-time rule is introduced.

decisionNodes.stem: Which examination protocol should evaluate {patientName}'s persistent upper-abdominal symptoms?

answerChoices.label: CT abdomen with intravenous contrast
answerChoices.rationale: Evaluates the pancreatic region, tissue enhancement and anatomic relationships when a post-pancreatitis complication is suspected.

answerChoices.label: CT abdomen with oral luminal contrast
answerChoices.rationale: Outlines the bowel but does not provide the same enhancement/vascular assessment of a pancreatic-region complication.

answerChoices.label: CT abdomen without contrast material
answerChoices.rationale: Can depict some findings, but does not provide equivalent tissue-enhancement information for characterizing the suspected complication.

decisionNodes.explanation: Persistent symptoms after pancreatitis require evaluation of possible structural complications. Contrast-enhanced CT characterizes the pancreatic region and its relationships; oral contrast or a noncontrast survey does not replace intravenous enhancement. MRI can also be appropriate in selected circumstances and is not offered as a falsely invalid alternative.

decisionNodes.stem: Which management plan should be recommended for {patientName}'s returned imaging findings and ongoing symptoms?

answerChoices.label: Referral for endoscopic transmural drainage assessment
answerChoices.rationale: Retains the passed anatomy/symptom inference while requiring specialist assessment of vascular/access safety before any puncture.

answerChoices.label: Referral for percutaneous catheter drainage assessment
answerChoices.rationale: Is a possible route in selected circumstances, but is not favored over endoscopic assessment for the supplied gastric apposition and burden.

answerChoices.label: Referral for operative internal drainage assessment
answerChoices.rationale: May be appropriate in selected anatomy or after other approaches fail; no such preference is established here.

answerChoices.label: Observation with nutritional support and repeat imaging
answerChoices.rationale: Is appropriate for some collections, but does not address the represented ongoing gastric compression/food-intake burden as well as specialist drainage planning.

decisionNodes.stem: Which test should be completed before {patientName}'s adrenal biopsy?

answerChoices.label: Plasma free metanephrines
answerChoices.rationale: Evaluates the catecholamine-related hazard before the planned invasive sampling.

answerChoices.label: Overnight dexamethasone suppression
answerChoices.rationale: Selects cortisol assessment from the adrenal hormonal workup rather than evaluating catecholamine secretion.

answerChoices.label: Plasma aldosterone-renin ratio
answerChoices.rationale: Selects a mineralocorticoid workup from a different adrenal decision pathway.

decisionNodes.explanation: Pheochromocytoma must be assessed before a biopsy of an indeterminate adrenal mass when tissue would change management. Plasma free metanephrines address that risk; urinary fractionated metanephrines are another accepted approach, but are not offered here. Cortisol or aldosterone evaluation answers different questions.

decisionNodes.stem: Which tissue-sampling plan should come first for {patientName}?

answerChoices.label: Ultrasound-guided core biopsy of parenchymal abnormality
answerChoices.rationale: Obtains tissue architecture from the imaged breast abnormality after an atypical cytologic sample; skin sampling can be adjunctive rather than a substitute for this target.

answerChoices.label: Ultrasound-guided aspiration of the parenchymal abnormality
answerChoices.rationale: Repeats a cytologic approach without repairing the limitation in establishing an invasive tissue diagnosis and biomarker material.

answerChoices.label: Punch sampling of the involved breast skin
answerChoices.rationale: Can provide useful adjunctive information but is not the best substitute for sampling the imaged parenchymal abnormality in this record.

decisionNodes.explanation: The rapidly evolving skin/breast findings warrant assessment of an invasive breast malignancy. Core tissue from the parenchymal abnormality addresses the inadequate cytologic material; skin punch may be adjunctive. The existing external pathway completes staging after confirmation, not because suspicion alone equals a cancer diagnosis.

decisionNodes.stem: If initial systemic therapy removes the palpable breast mass and skin changes, which local treatment plan should be retained for {patientName}?

answerChoices.rationale: Uses the original inflammatory cancer presentation and curative stage rather than assuming a clinical response permits omission or de-escalation of required local treatment.

answerChoices.rationale: Mistakes clinical downstaging for permission to substitute breast conservation in the represented inflammatory cancer pathway.

answerChoices.rationale: Mistakes an apparent clinical response for justification to reserve surgery for salvage.

decisionNodes.stem: Which evaluation plan should guide {patientName}'s next visit?

answerChoices.label: Breast assessment and medication review
answerChoices.rationale: Recognizes a focal concerning component alongside a plausible systemic explanation for the expressed bilateral secretion; an elevated prolactin does not explain away the focal episodes.

answerChoices.label: Medication review and symptom reassessment
answerChoices.rationale: Over-unifies the observed patterns under a real prolactin-raising medicine and postpones assessment of the focal component.

answerChoices.label: Endocrine assessment and medication review
answerChoices.rationale: Overweights the laboratory abnormality and treats it as a sufficient explanation for all of the breast observations.

decisionNodes.explanation: A medication-related prolactin rise can account for bilateral secretion, while spontaneous unilateral duct discharge still warrants breast-local assessment. The two patterns can coexist; do not assume one systemic finding explains both.

decisionNodes.stem: Which examination protocol should be ordered next for {patientName}?

answerChoices.label: Hepatobiliary scintigraphy assessing gallbladder filling
answerChoices.rationale: Persistent local inflammatory findings call for assessment of gallbladder filling/cystic-duct obstruction despite the ultrasound components.

answerChoices.label: Hepatobiliary scintigraphy measuring stimulated ejection fraction
answerChoices.rationale: Confuses evaluation of chronic gallbladder emptying with evaluation of the acute inflammatory presentation.

answerChoices.label: MR cholangiopancreatography assessing the extrahepatic ducts
answerChoices.rationale: Prioritizes a duct-stone question over the gallbladder question suggested by persistent local signs; it is not a claim that MRI is never appropriate after ultrasound.

decisionNodes.explanation: The clinical findings maintain concern for acute gallbladder inflammation. A filling study addresses cystic-duct obstruction; a stimulated ejection-fraction study addresses a different physiologic question. MRCP is a duct-focused protocol, not a universal substitute for either. Interpret any scan with preparation and technical limitations in mind.

decisionNodes.stem: Which phosphate movement best accounts for the fall in serum phosphate during this nutrition restart?

answerChoices.label: From extracellular fluid into cells
answerChoices.rationale: Connects carbohydrate-driven insulin activity with cellular phosphate uptake.

answerChoices.label: From cells into extracellular fluid
answerChoices.rationale: Reverses the compartment shift and would tend to raise the measured extracellular concentration.

answerChoices.label: From circulating blood into urine
answerChoices.rationale: Mistakes an intracellular redistribution for renal loss after focusing on the falling serum result.

answerChoices.label: From intestinal lumen into blood
answerChoices.rationale: Confuses the source of newly absorbed nutrients with the redistribution explaining the serum fall.

decisionNodes.explanation: After prolonged undernutrition, carbohydrate-associated insulin activity can increase cellular phosphate uptake. The relevant movement is from extracellular fluid into cells; the serum result measures the extracellular compartment.

decisionNodes.stem: Which combined medication plan should be agreed with {patientName}'s surgical team?

answerChoices.label: Continue ART; plan titrated intravenous midazolam with respiratory monitoring
answerChoices.rationale: Preserves ART continuity and uses the route for which monitored, individualized midazolam administration can be considered with a boosted regimen.

answerChoices.label: Continue ART; plan oral midazolam with respiratory monitoring
answerChoices.rationale: Preserves continuity but treats monitoring as sufficient to make the contraindicated oral combination acceptable.

answerChoices.label: Interrupt ART; plan titrated intravenous midazolam with respiratory monitoring
answerChoices.rationale: Changes a complete regimen unnecessarily instead of coordinating the interacting procedural medicine.

answerChoices.label: Interrupt ART; plan oral midazolam with respiratory monitoring
answerChoices.rationale: Both interrupts treatment and assumes an unspecified interruption makes the oral interaction acceptable.

decisionNodes.explanation: Coordinate ART continuity and procedural medicines with the HIV/anesthesia teams. Oral midazolam should not be coadministered with a boosted protease-inhibitor regimen; parenteral use needs appropriate monitoring, individualized titration and consideration of dose reduction. No interruption or washout interval is assumed here.

cases.learningSummary: The correct answer is “Continue ART with the perioperative team.” Routine surgery alone is not an indication to stop effective ART. Surgical recovery alone does not justify interrupting feasible ART. An uncoordinated single-drug substitute does not preserve the prescribed regimen. Uncoordinated removal of part of a regimen is not the continuity plan. The correct answer is “Revise sedation for the ART interaction.” Boosted therapy can increase midazolam exposure; this oral combination requires an alternative plan. The oral combination has a route-specific contraindication. Increased exposure from metabolic inhibition does not support a dose increase. A coordinated alternative sedation plan is preferable to sacrificing feasible effective ART.

cases.learningSummary: The correct answer is “Irritant contact dermatitis.” The leakage distribution and wet erosions support an effluent-related irritant process. Spreading erythema and other infection findings are absent in this story. No fungal-pattern findings are described; leakage explains this injury. A deep, progressive undermined ulcer is not described. The correct answer is “Refit the seal with ostomy-nurse guidance.” Fit correction and compatible skin protection address the continuing exposure. Antibiotics do not correct continuing noninfectious leakage. A fungal pattern is not supplied, and the leaking fit remains the cause. An enlarged opening exposes more skin to effluent.
